title: The giant transformers that keep a power grid running can take years to replace
body: On 14 October 2026 Kyiv’s mayor said missile strikes on energy facilities had cut power in the city, [Meduza reported](https://meduza.io/en/news/2026/10/14/russian-strike-on-kyiv-kills-three-injures-over-20-parts-of-city-lose-power). Repairing a grid is slow partly because of its biggest machines. Transformers step the voltage from power stations up to hundreds of thousands of volts for long lines, and back down again for homes. At a higher voltage the same power needs less current, and since wires lose energy as heat in proportion to the current squared, ten times the voltage means a hundredth of the loss. The largest transformers weigh 100 to 400 tons, are built to order for one site and travel on special rail cars. In the US a new one now often takes three years to arrive, according to the [Department of Energy](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2024-10/EXEC-2022-001242%20-%20Large%20Power%20Transformer%20Resilience%20Report%207-10-24.pdf), which is why grid companies keep spares and share them.

slides.question: In the US today, how long does a new large power transformer often take to arrive after it is ordered?
slides.explanation: About 36 months is commonly quoted, and up to 60, says the US Department of Energy (2024). Before the pandemic, under a year was possible.

slides.alt: Animation on a dark slate night: a city's windows go dark, then a big transformer. Voltage steps up and down from station to homes; a thick wire at 10 kV glows with heat, a thin one at 100 kV barely; pylons; coils on an iron core; the weight, custom designs, a 36-month wait and a special rail car.
slides.music: “On My Way” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Power leaves a 10 kV generator. Step up the line voltage until less than 1% of the 10 MW is lost as heat.
slides.takeaway: Above about 71 kV the loss drops under 1%. Each tenfold rise in voltage cuts the current tenfold and the heat a hundredfold. Without a step-up transformer, half the power would be lost here.

slides.heading: Heat lost sending 10 MW down a 5-ohm line
Why not keep spares of everything?
slides.text: Large transformers often cost millions of dollars, and each is built for the voltages and layout of one site, so a spare for one place may not fit another. Grid companies keep some and run schemes to lend them out, and the US Department of Energy has studied a national reserve.

slides.question: Why do long-distance power lines run at very high voltage?
options: Less current, so less heat lost
It keeps the wires cool in summer
slides.explanation: Power is voltage times current, and wires lose heat in proportion to the current squared. Ten times the voltage means a tenth of the current and a hundredth of the loss.
